1. Core Clinical Tension: A 45-year-old previously healthy male presents with a subacute 2-week history of fever, headache, and progressive neurological deterioration into stupor and coma. The severe intracranial hypertension (>330 mmH2O), marked meningismus, and leukocytosis resemble acute bacterial meningitis, but the subacute time course, failure of outpatient fluoroquinolone/cephalosporin therapy, apical fibrocalcific pulmonary nodules, and neuroimaging showing hydrocephalus with basal meningeal enhancement strongly point to tuberculous meningitis with obstructive hydrocephalus.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint is set immediately following admission physical and neurological examination, triage blood labs (elevated WBC, CRP, ESR; normal organ function), brain MRI and chest CT findings, and admission lumbar puncture demonstrating opening pressure >330 mmH2O, elevated protein (2610 mg/dL), pleocytosis (375x10^6/L), and severe hypoglycorrhachia, immediately prior to send-out molecular testing (GeneXpert MTB/RIF) and surgical drain placement.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute bacterial meningitis has a fulminant hyperacute course and neutrophilic CSF, whereas this patient had a 2-week indolent course failing empiric cephalosporin/levofloxacin. Viral meningoencephalitis presents with normal CSF glucose and modest protein elevation, directly contradicted by this patient's extreme hypoglycorrhachia (CSF:serum ratio <0.21) and protein >2000 mg/dL. Fungal (cryptococcal) meningitis shares intracranial hypertension and subacute onset, but tuberculous meningitis is strongly favored by concurrent apical calcified pulmonary nodules and confirmed by mycobacterial nucleic acid amplification.
case_prompt:
A 45-year-old Chinese male presented in a comatose state following a two-week history of progressively worsening headache, intermittent high fever (38.5°C to 39.0°C), nausea, and profound fatigue. Two weeks prior to presentation, he had sought outpatient medical care, where initial blood counts, routine urinalysis, and rapid antigen testing for influenza A and B viruses were normal. He was treated empirically with oral cefuroxime and levofloxacin for five days, but his fever and headache persisted and his mental status progressively deteriorated. He had a history of tobacco use, did not consume alcohol, had no prior chronic medical conditions, and reported no travel in the past six months.

Because of progressive obtundation, he was admitted to a community hospital where initial investigations were performed. An initial lumbar puncture revealed an elevated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein level of 2155 mg/dL and a depressed CSF glucose level of 0.85 mmol/L (reference: 2.22–3.89 mmol/L). Computed tomography of the chest revealed nodules with calcification in the right upper lobe, along with airspace consolidations in both lower lobes. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated ventriculomegaly, diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement, and obstructive hydrocephalus. He was urgently transferred to a tertiary center for specialized neuro-infectious evaluation.

Upon arrival at the tertiary center, physical examination demonstrated a body temperature of 37.1°C, heart rate of 166 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 52 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 159/119 mmHg. Neurological examination revealed severe encephalopathy with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 (E2V2M3), marked neck stiffness, and a positive Kernig sign, without focal motor, sensory, or cerebellar deficits.

Laboratory testing revealed a peripheral white blood cell count of 17.07 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 29.12 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 59 mm/h. Serum electrolytes, renal function, and hepatic function were within normal limits. A repeat lumbar puncture revealed a CSF opening pressure exceeding 330 mmH2O. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated a white cell count of 375 × 10^6/L, protein of 2610 mg/dL, and glucose of 1.95 mmol/L, with a simultaneous serum glucose of 9.4 mmol/L.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because of the pronounced meningismus, severe intracranial hypertension, elevated inflammatory markers, and markedly depressed CSF glucose. However, pyogenic meningitis typically progresses hyperacutely over hours to days rather than exhibiting a subacute two-week prodrome, and it failed to respond to empiric outpatient therapy with cefuroxime and levofloxacin.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He was prescribed an empirical antibiotic therapy with Levofloxacin and Cefuroxime for five days. However, his fever, headache, and fatigue persisted, and his consciousness worsened.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered initially given the acute constitutional syndrome of fever, headache, nausea, and fatigue. Ruled out by negative rapid influenza testing, marked CSF opening pressure (>330 mmH2O), extreme CSF protein elevation (>2600 mg/dL), and severe hypoglycorrhachia (CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.21), which are incompatible with uncomplicated viral central nervous system infections.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: His blood routine examination, rapid antigen test for type A/B flu virus, and routine urine examination were all normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the subacute presentation, marked intracranial hypertension (>330 mmH2O), meningeal enhancement, and ventriculomegaly/hydrocephalus. However, the presence of apical calcified lung nodules and consolidations raised high suspicion for mycobacterial infection, and rapid molecular assays established the specific bacterial etiology.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed ventriculomegaly, meningeal enhancement and hydrocephalus (Figure 2A-D). A diagnosis of TBM was highly suspected and he was transferred to our hospital.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot occurred when GeneXpert MTB/RIF testing on the cerebrospinal fluid returned positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA with detected rifampicin resistance, confirming pre-extensive drug-resistant tuberculous meningitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: GeneXpert MTB/RIF results of CSF were positive (semi-quantitative result: Medium) for TB-DNA with resistance to rifampicin.

editor_comments: Admission breakpoint placed following physical exam, admission blood labs, brain MRI, chest CT, and admission LP parameters, stopping strictly before GeneXpert molecular testing. Verbatim quotes from source text verify differential rule-outs and diagnostic pivot. Target canonical disease Tuberculosis verified.
